b: There’s an atmospheric, weather-beaten quality to Lottie Brazier’s On Course But No-One There To Salute You, a debut album that dons a rain mac and steps out gingerly to face the elements. Arriving as it does as the autumn falls away, it feels somehow seasonally appropriate like a new winter coat, making it all the more melancholic and evocative when the clouds are replete with blackness and the rain can be heard tapping away at the roof. That’s certainly true of opener ‘Look Outside’, which briefly comes over the hill like a more ambient Vangelis track before settling into something more windswept and emotionally complicated, driven by Brazier’s androgynous, multitracked vocals.

Recording these eleven songs between her home and the studios of 4AD in Wandsworth, that combination of self-reliance and doffing a cap to the gods and goddesses of echo is evident in every delay-treated bar. We’re not beholden here to artists like the Cocteau Twins or Throwing Muses, though this album would unlikely exist without them. That lineage and that history is important to the slow creation of this work, as is place. Most of the songs were reared in her native Suffolk some years ago, where the landscape – the shingle beaches and the crumbling cliffs – inform these romantic, down-at-heel songs, a youthful weariness caught in a mid-80s vortex that somehow also sounds timeless.

On Course… is whimsical enough to have come from the 4AD stable, but there’s a hard-edged clarity to many of the lyrics that bat away overused, wishy-washy descriptors like “ethereal”: “These are not your better days and I am not your muse,” she chides on ‘Ropes of Time’, “Please make no compromise / you know I cannot be for show.” Moreover, the relatively upbeat, jagged-edged ‘Take A Bow’ was written whilst Brazier was living in Brighton where she experienced a sense of creative release.

As a student of avant-pop and a writer for The Wire (as well as on these very pages), there’s a sense that it’s taken a lot of effort for her to make music this effortless; as flowing as it is fastidious, respectful of a rich vein of influences while attempting to move forwards in her own way. Centre-piece ‘Redshift’ is surely the most experimental track here, an arpeggiated analogue synth epic that threatens to come undone as instruments are starkly and ruthlessly omitted with the unfurling of the song, creating a tension as gaps of silence emerge.

That song is offset by the more offbeat, catchy, Smiths-like ‘Working On A Sunday’, which captures the ennui of trying to keep busy in order to forget someone’s face. Brazier wrote and produced all of these songs, and that sense of solitude is apparent. There’s a touch of ambivalence, but it’s also a contained and even contented ambivalence, as the final song ‘Do You Want To Be Lonely’ attests. In that sense, the songs feel like epistles or dispatches, written with care in front of the fire, before the protagonist heads out to the bleak Jarman-esque coastline to face up to the battering rain.
